items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the labor law, in relation to establishing the warehouse
worker protection act
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8922

SPONSOR: RAMOS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the labor law, in relation to establishing the warehouse
worker protection act

 
PURPOSE:

Relates to the creation of a program to protect workers from unreason-
able quotas and to reduce workplace injuries via a new section of Labor
Law. This bill will support warehouse workers who currently have no
protections from inhumane work quotas and also lack workplace ergonomics
standards.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: This Act shall be known as the "warehouse worker protection
act"

Section 2: Legislative findings.

Section 3: The labor law is amended by adding a new article 21-a as
follows:

Section 780 Definitions. Provides all definitions.

Section 781 Quotas. Establishes transparency standards for the provision
to each employee the quota to which they are subject and any conse-
quences for failure to meet the quota.

Section 782 Protection from Quotas. Quotas may not interfere with a
worker meeting basic human needs, like meal or rest periods, use of
bathroom and preventing workplace injury.

Section 783 Time on Task. Time on task must include:

1) an employee's actions to minimize risk of injury; and

2) Paid and unpaid breaks are not considered productive time.

Section 784 Right to Request.

1.

a. Current and former employees have the right to request the quota to
which they are subject as well as work speed data.

b. Former employees may receive 6 months of former employee's quotas and
work speed data.

2. Employers have two business days to comply with request made in part
a.

3. Employers are not required to use quotas or monitor work speed data.
If an employer does not monitor, then no obligation to provide it upon
request.

Section 785 Injury Reduction Program. Each employer shall establish this
program to identify and minimize the risk of musculoskeletal injuries
and disorders.

1. Worksite Evaluation. Each job shall have a written work site evalu-
ation by a qualified ergonomist.

a. Evaluation shall include whether there are quotas in place;

b. Evaluation shall include worker recommendations on risk factors and
changes to be made to reduce risk;

c. Copies of evaluation shall be made available to workers;

d. Evaluation shall be conducted within 3 months of effective data and
updated annually;

e. Within 6 months of enactment, the Commissioner shall create standards
to determine certification for qualified ergonomists.

2. Control of risk factors that have caused or are likely to cause
musculoskeletal injuries and disorders. Employer shall correct any risk
factors identified in a timely manner.

a. Where eliminating risk cannot be done, employer shall minimize expo-
sure to risk;

b. To reduce risk factors, employer shall consider: i. engineering
controls and workstation redesign;

ii. Administrative controls;

c. Records of steps taken to eliminate or reduce risk

3. Training. Employers must provide injury reduction training to employ-
ees, including:

a. Symptoms of musculoskeletal injuries;

b. Musculoskeletal injury risk factors and exposures;

c. Methods to reduce risk factors; d. Employer's program to identify
risk factors;

e. Rights and functions of Workplace Safety Committees and the right to
report;

f. Unlawful retaliation provisions.

4. Medical Management. Medical professionals operating under legal scope
of practice must staff any on-site medical office or first aid station.

a. Employer must assure such staffing meets New York State requirements;

b. Employers must consult with a NY State-Licensed Physician Board-Cer-
tified in Occupational Medicine if workers must be seen by on-site
medical providers prior to going to doctor;

i. Medical consultant shall conduct evaluation of on-site medical
management program;

ii. Medical consultant shall provide a summary of treatment protocols;

iii. Medical consultant shall review evaluation annually;

iv. Designated medical providers shall observe all jobs in the ware-
house;

c. No unnecessary delays in provision of adequate medical care;

d. No discrimination or retaliation for reporting work-related injury or
illness.

5. Employee Involvement. Employer shall consult employees and designated
representatives to develop and implement all aspects of this program.

Section 786. Unlawful Retaliation.

1. No person shall retaliate against a person for exercising rights
conferred under this act, including;

a. Initiating a request for information;

b. Making a complaint related to a quota;

c. Making a complaint related to Injury Reduction Program.

2. Employee does not need to refer to this Act to be protected.

3. Rebuttable presumption if adverse action taken against a worker with-
in 9 days of engaging in activities protected by this Act. Clear and
convincing evidence must show that,

a. The adverse action was taken for other permissible reasons; and

b. The activities protected by this act were not motivating factor in
adverse action.

Section 787. Subpoena. Commissioner may request or subpoena employer
records and data upon receipt of complaint regarding a violation of this
section.

Section 788. Enforcement.

1. Commissioner shall enforce this law

2.

a. Employees or employee representatives may request an inspection of a
facility by the commissioner. Such request shall be:

i. Made in writing;

ii. Specific;

iii. Signed;
iv. Provided to employer upon inspection by commissioner

b. Inspections shall be made within three days of receipt of notice by
Commissioner.

3. Employer and employee representatives may accompany the commissioner
during an inspection.

4. Commissioner may inspect any aspect of facility where there is reason
to believe a violation exists.

5. Employees accompanying commissioner on inspection shall not lose
wages.

6. Commissioner may conduct inspection upon own initiative.

7. If request for inspection has been made based on imminent danger, the
inspection shall be carried out immediately.

8. If commissioner finds a violation, within 6 months shall issue an
order to comply. Penalties for failure to comply are set.

9. Orders to comply shall be posted at the workplace.

10. Employers and employees may petition the industrial board of appeals
for review of determinations, followed by judicial review.

11. Commissioner can seek judicial enforcement of an order to comply.

12.

a. Where conditions could reasonably be expected to cause serious phys-
ical harm immediately, the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to restrain
any practices prohibited under this section.

b. Inspector shall inform employees of any dangers and recommendations
if inspector finds they exist in accordance with paragraph a.

c. If commissioner does not seek relief under this section within 48
hours of notification of such a condition, employees may seek injunctive
relief.

13. Commissioner shall provide a report one year after enactment to the
legislature.

14. If a worksite has annual employee injury rate at least 1.5 times as
high as the warehouse industry average, the commissions shall conduct an
investigation.

15. Commissioner may adopt regulations.

16. If the commissioner brings a successful action to enforce this part,
the court may grant injunctive relief to obtain compliance and shall
award costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

Section 789. Private Right of Action. Employees may bring an action for
injunctive relief to obtain compliance with this Act and may recover
costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Sets limitations on awards.
Section 790. Records. Any records collected based on investigations
under this section shall be made public, although personally identifi-
able information may be protected.

Section 791. Other Powers. The Attorney General may prosecute actions
for violations of this section.

Section 4. Severability. Provisions are severable.

Section 5. Effective Date. 60 days after it becomes law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

a) The rapid growth of just-in-time logistics and same and next-day
consumer package delivery, and advances in technology used for tracking
employee productivity, have led to a rise in the number of warehouse and
distribution center workers who are subject to quantified work quotas.

(b) Warehouse and distribution center employees who work under those
quotas are expected to complete a quantified number of tasks within
specific time periods, often measured down to the minute or second, and
face adverse employment action, including suspension or termination, if
they fail to do so.

(c) Those quotas generally do not allow for workers to comply with safe-
ty guidelines or to recover from strenuous activity during productive
work time, leaving warehouse and distribution center employees who work
under them at high risk of injury and illness.

(d) The quotas under which warehouse and distribution center employees
regularly work also affect their compensation. Warehouse and distrib-
ution center employees who work under a quota may not receive the full
benefit of minimum wages if their quota is increased to make up for the
direct or indirect effect of a minimum-wage increase.

(e) Quotas in occupations that are already physically demanding incen-
tivize unsafe work, resulting in an increase in injuries. The workforce
in warehouse and logistics is largely comprised of people of color who
depend upon these jobs to provide for their families and often see no
alternative but to prioritize quota compliance over their own safety.
These workers end up working faster than is healthy in order to keep
their jobs.

(f) Workplace injuries can take a terrible toll on workers, their fami-
lies and their communities, and can create substantial costs for employ-
ers. According to the most recent data (2020) released by the Bureau of
Labor Statistics, the warehouse industry itself reports a rate of seri-
ous work-related injuries involving lost time or restricted duty (4.0
cases/100 full-time workers) that is more than twice the average injury
rates for all private industry (1.7 cases/100 FTE's). The most common
types of work-related serious injury reported by employers in the ware-
house sector are musculoskeletal injuries (MSDs), which often require
workers to miss work and can force workers permanently out of the job
and even out of the workforce.

(g) Warehouse companies often require workers to perform fast paced
manual material handling tasks. These involve well-known risk factors
for serious injury such as rapid pace, repetitive forceful exertions
like lifting heavy packages, and awkward postures like twisting/bending,
and combinations thereof that are likely to cause MSDs. Scientific
evidence shows that effective ergonomic interventions --such as reducing
the pace, package weights and stressful postures--can lower the inci-
dence and severity of work-related MSDs. The research is clear that the
most effective method for reducing or eliminating these risk factors is
to implement an ergonomics program that includes well-informed analysis
of the worksite, implementation of solutions to reduce the dangerous
risk factors, professionally competent medical management, effective
worker training, and meaningful involvement by workers and their repre-
sentatives in all aspects of the program.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

FY 2023: N/A

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect 60 days after it shall become law.

BILL NUMBER: S8922A                REVISED 5/27/22

SPONSOR: RAMOS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

worker protection act

 
PURPOSE:

1. Paid and unpaid breaks are not considered productive time for the

Section 784 Recordkeeping.

Each employer shall track and preserve records related to, a. Each
employees work speed data, b. Aggregate work speed data, and c.  Written

Section 785 Right to Request.

1. Current employees have the right to request data relevant to the
employee's quota.

2. Former employees may request within three years of separation from
employer data relevant to the employee's quota.

3. Records shall be provided at no cost to current or former employee.

4. Employers shall provide quota descriptions no later than two days
after request. Employers shall provide personal work speed data and
aggregated work speed no later than seven business days following the
request.

5. Employers are not required to use quotas or monitor work speed data.
If an employer does not monitor, then no obligation to provide it upon
request.

Section 786. Unlawful Retaliation.

1. No person shall retaliate against a person for exercising rights

mation; b. Making a complaint related to a quota;

2. Employees do not need to refer to this Act to be protected.

convincing evidence must show that, a. The adverse action was taken for
other permissible reasons; and b. The activities protected by this act
were not a motivating factor in adverse action.

Section 787. Enforcement.

1. Commissioner shall adopt rules and regulations implementing this
article, shall be authorized to enforce this article, and to assess
civil penalties consistent to sections 213, 215 and 218 of this chapter.

Section 788. Other Powers. The Attorney General may prosecute actions
for violations of this section.

Section 4. Severability. Provisions are severable.

Section 5. Effective Date. 60 days after it becomes law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

advances in technology used for tracking employee productivity, have led
to a rise in the number of warehouse and distribution center workers who

Warehouse companies often require workers to perform fast paced manual

ous injury such as rapid pace, repetitive forceful exertions like lift-
ing heavy packages, and awkward postures like twisting/bending, and

and severity of work-related MSDs. The research is clear that the most

the worksite, implementation of solutions to reduce the dangerous risk
factors, professionally competent medical management, effective worker
training, and meaningful involvement by workers and their represen-
tatives in all aspects of the program.

This legislation puts safeguards on the algorithms which are monitoring,
punishing and pushing workers to burn out or get injured.  The legis-
lation prevents the algorithm from placing workloads on employees that
could injure the worker. Every workplace will have an ergonomic assess-
ment of all tasks and based on that assessment will be provided safe
workloads. Second, the bill creates penalties and enforcement mechanism
at DOL against workers are provided access to the quotas and algorithms
that are regulating their work;

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

FY 2023: N/A

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect 60 days after it shall become law.

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 44 Chapter 722
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 8922-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend  the  labor law, in relation to establishing the
        warehouse worker protection act"
 
    APPROVED
 
  This bill would require  covered  warehouse  distribution  centers  to
disclose  work speed data to its current and former employees and estab-
lish protections from adverse employment actions based  on  failures  to
meet  undisclosed  speed  quotas  or  quotas that do not allow employees
proper breaks.
 
  I fully support providing greater protections for workers, but I  have
concerns about the extent of the impact that this legislation could have
on  businesses.  I have therefore reached an agreement with the Legisla-
ture to resolve these concerns. First, key  terms  including  "employee"
and  "employer"  have  been  clarified. These clarifications will ensure
that the bill's provisions clearly  only  apply  to  warehouse  workers.
Second,  the  parameters for requesting quota information and responding
to such requests have been simplified to assist employers, and  finally,
amendments  have  been  made to clarify the anti-retaliation provisions,
address employee language access,  make  technical  corrections  to  the
enforcement provisions, and allow more time for employers to effectively
implement this new law.
 
  Based on this agreement, I am pleased to sign this bill into law.
 
  This bill is approved.                         (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______

summary: Establishes the warehouse worker protection act; requires employers to provide a written description of quotas to which employees are subject and states that employees shall not be required to meet quotas that prevent compliance with meal or rest periods, or use of bathroom facilities.
title: Establishes the warehouse worker protection act
